276.history: The eldest of the three wells that claim the mason's crack is the home of Clann na Ceiste, who keep lines longer than any roll. Cailean mac Eachainn walked the hill road there in the hundred and twenty-sixth year with seven names copied on a scrap of paper inside his coat, to ask whether a line so old could truly be Donnchadh's own, and came back with Sloinneadh Aisling. Its water runs along a straight stone channel through the village, and the keepers of the lines there asked Cailean nothing in return but that the line be copied fair.
276.known_for: the keepers of the long lines

212.history: The old mill of the north, whose wheel Clàr nan Rìghrean already calls ancient, took Merriman's first constable post in the hundred and thirty-second year, a stone house with a yard for horses on the northern coal road. The townsfolk called it the humans' second Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and did not mean it kindly. In the first week of the rising the post was taken at first light and its constables sent south on foot. Its walls went up in the years of the constables, around the post and the mill together, and its miller ground for the post and for the town at the same price.

438.history: The village of the blue spring holds the greatest wool fairs of the north, older than the strangers' coming. A second constable post was raised there in the hundred and thirty-third year near the northern workings; its custodian was paid rent for the ground, and with it bought the village out of its debts to A' Chompanaidh's store. The post fell with Muileann shean's in the first week of the rising. The humans' wool-buyers came to its fairs every year of the age, and paid in marks once the coin was struck.
438.known_for: the wool fairs, and the rent that paid the store

86.history: The harbour on the low strait of the north coast has salt pans that supply the northern fisheries. The blasting-powder for the new deep galleries was landed there in the hundred and thirty-sixth year, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard; the custodians asked what was in the barrels and were told it was lamp-oil. It keeps the ancestor rite of the old coast, and its custodians wrote the lamp-oil into their roll with the weight the carters said the barrels had.

389.history: The narrow field was built by the people of the district A' Chompanaidh fenced and closed after Scàineadh Cill ghlas, on common ground lent them by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. They raised it through a spring and summer without a single A' Chompanaidh's surveyor setting foot on it: a well dug first, then the custodian's house, then the households in the order their names were drawn at the stone. Its shrine-keepers lit a new lamp without the old keeper's name on it. It stands on the edge of the fenced ground, and from its well the wire of the closed district can be seen along the slope.
389.founded_by: the dispossessed of the closed district
389.known_for: a village built without a surveyor

29.history: The harbour on the capital shore, eighteen miles down the river from Ros dhomhain, shut the only quay it had for the coal traffic in the season of the flux and let no barge tie up; it paid A' Chompanaidh's fine from the purse that had buried its dead. Anne Colby walked there to help lay out the last of them. In Stad-oibre a' Chalaidh of the hundred and thirty-fourth year its dockers, with no human among them, refused to load the coal sent round to them; they were not shipped over the sea, but neither were they hired again for two years. It stands on the old quay stones of the Seann-Dhaoine, still seen at low water, and its harbour-master's rolls show its dockers unhired two years running.
29.known_for: the quay shut against the flux
